characters.intro: Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to Hollowmere! Yes, it is mine. Yes, all of it, including the damp. I am Sir Jonathan Reginald Pemberwick, property investor, visionary, and as of this spring the owner of forty-one bedrooms, nine of which still have roofs. Tonight I have gathered my oldest friends to celebrate the Order our families founded, and to announce the estate covenant: twelve million pounds, to be shared among us. Don't thank me. Well, do, a little. As your host I naturally have the final word on everything, which my wife assures me is not how marriage works.

secret.title: The Hidden Will
secret.text: When your great-uncle died, you found a later will among his papers leaving Hollowmere's farms to your cousin Thomas Pemberwick. You burned it. The older will stood, the estate came to you whole, and Thomas emigrated to Canada with nothing.
secret.excuse: Thomas would have sold the farms within a year. You kept Hollowmere together. Somebody had to.
secret.proof: A copy of the later will, witnessed by Silas himself on the day it was signed.

characters.need_alive: Silas knows where the authoritative deed to the manor is kept. With it, the Ravenscroft claim to part of the estate collapses.

scandal.text: Nanor owes large sums to half the people in this room while pretending to be fabulously solvent.

memories: You and Grant were wrestling over who got to hold the spirit board when somebody's elbow caught the candelabra. It went over onto the papers. You have always been certain it was Grant's elbow. You have never been entirely certain.

s1.truth: In my place in the circle, on the north side, between Danielle and the altar end.
s1.lie: I went to the side table to find a candle.

s2.truth: Danielle was on my left. She'd know if I'd moved.
s2.lie: Half the room. Everyone could see me.

s3.truth: Behind the Black Hound last night. He wanted me to disclose an old estate schedule before the ceremony. I lost my temper.
s3.lie: Pleasantries. He asked after the roof.

s4.truth: I confronted Silas behind the inn about an old beneficiary schedule. I said things I regret.
s4.lie: I was at home going over the guest list.

s5.truth: Silas polished it before the ceremony and made a show of setting it on the stand. I joked he should sell it.

characters.blackout: The thunder shook the floor under your feet. In the dark you heard Silas begin a word, 'Wh-', and then a dull, heavy sound, like a sack set down hard.
characters.last_word: Silas favoured you as a boy. Tonight you found out he was planning to put you on trial.

characters.intro: Good evening, darlings. Lady Danielle Pemberwick: hostess, art collector, and the only person in this house who knows which fork is for the fish. I have hung every painting at Hollowmere myself, twice, because Jonathan hung them the first time. I collect beautiful things and I keep them. That includes secrets, so do be careful what you tell me after the second glass. Tonight I intend to be gracious, charming and utterly unbothered, and if anything embarrassing happens I shall simply pretend it was planned.

secret.title: The Forged Farewell
secret.text: When your younger sister Rose fell in love with a penniless painter, Daniel Hale, you forged a letter in her hand breaking off the engagement. He left for Paris believing she had rejected him. Rose has never been happy since, and she has never known why he went.
secret.excuse: He had nothing. You saved her from a garret and a lifetime of debt. You were the sensible one. You always are.
secret.proof: Your practice sheets, copying Rose's handwriting line by line.

characters.need_alive: Silas knows where Daniel Hale lives now. If you are ever going to put it right, you need him.

scandal.text: Grant pawned an heirloom of Caroline's to cover gambling debts, and has been wearing a paste copy ever since.

memories: Eleanor didn't want to go to the séance. You told her that if she refused, you would tell Silas she had stolen your hair ribbons. She came, crying. You have never told a soul why Eleanor was in that room that night.

s1.truth: In my place on the north side, between Nanor and Jonathan.
s1.lie: I stepped toward the vestry door. There was a draught.

s2.truth: Jonathan on one side, Nanor on the other.
s2.lie: My husband was holding my hand the whole time.

s3.truth: Yesterday, in his rooms. He handed me back my grandmother's brooch and told me to stop hiding things from Jonathan.
s3.lie: We discussed the flowers for tonight.

s4.truth: I collected a family heirloom from Silas's rooms, a brooch I had pawned and redeemed through him. Jonathan doesn't know.
s4.lie: I was at the dressmaker's, then at home.

s5.truth: It was on its stand when I arrived. The stand has a little velvet cushion. I noticed the velvet was dusty.

characters.blackout: The moment the lights died you smelled hot candle wax, and you felt a cold draught across your ankles, as if a door had opened somewhere behind you.
characters.last_word: Silas helped you hide a debt from your husband. Kindly. Which means he knows exactly where your secrets are kept.

characters.intro: Lord Grant Bartholomew Blackthorne the Third, estate surveyor and cartographer. I have measured this house. Twice. It is eleven inches wider than the plans claim, and somebody owes me an explanation. I believe every dispute in human history could have been settled with a theodolite and a little patience. Wars, marriages, the matter of who took the last sherry. Tonight I shall be watching, measuring and taking notes, and if anyone moves the furniture I will know.

secret.title: The Warning
secret.text: In 1888 you received an engineer's signed warning that the Millbrook viaduct's foundations were unsound. You had money in the scheme, so you filed the warning away. The viaduct cracked, the line was closed for a year, and the junior engineer, Arthur Penn, was blamed and dismissed. Nobody was killed. You remind yourself of that often.
secret.excuse: Engineers always cry wolf. The warning was speculative. You had no way of knowing.
secret.proof: The original warning, in an envelope with your own handwriting on it: 'File. Not to be shown.'

characters.need_alive: Silas knows where the original Blackthorne boundary plans are kept. Without them, a neighbour's challenge could take a third of your land.

scandal.text: Grace knowingly sold a counterfeit Roman bronze to a duke as genuine.

memories: You were the only one who knew the secret passage behind the library, so you led everyone into the east wing. Then you wedged a chair under the records-room door so no grown-up could walk in on you. When the fire started, everyone fled down your passage in single file, in the dark. Eleanor was the smallest, and she was furthest from it.

s1.truth: In my place on the south side, at the altar end, beside Caroline.
s1.lie: I went out to check the lamps.

s2.truth: Caroline. She was on my left.
s2.lie: Everyone. I'm very hard to miss.

s3.truth: He asked whether I'd ever found the old plans of the chapel passage. Odd question. I said no.
s3.lie: We spoke about the weather. It was going to storm.

s4.truth: Surveying the grounds after dark. The exterior lamps were failing, so I went down to the electrical panel and fixed a loose fuse. I hid when I heard someone coming, because it isn't my house.
s4.lie: I was in my room reading.

s5.truth: I measured it, if you must know. Fourteen inches, broad blade. It was on the stand at nine o'clock.

characters.blackout: By the luminous hands of your pocket watch, the lights were out for almost exactly two minutes. You counted the seconds out of habit. You could not see your own hands.
characters.last_word: Silas has the one document that could ruin your reputation, and the one map that could save your land.

characters.intro: Lady Caroline Blackthorne, botanist. Fellow of absolutely everything. I have grown orchids that the Royal Horticultural Society said could not be grown, and I've won the gold medal three years running, which some people find hard to forgive. If you have a garden, I have opinions about it. If you have roses, I'm sorry. My husband measures things; I make them grow. Between us we are unbearable, and we know it.

secret.title: The Blighted Garden
secret.text: Before the Royal medal of 1889 you crept into your rival Agatha Fenn's orchid house and treated her plants with a blight of your own devising. Her collection died. Worse, people decided she had smuggled diseased plants, and she was disgraced. You won the medal.
secret.excuse: She was a fraud in all but name, and you were the better botanist. You only hurried along the inevitable.
secret.proof: An apothecary's ledger showing your purchases, and your own notes for the blight formula.

characters.need_alive: Silas holds your notes proving that the remedy you gave him last night was harmless feverfew and willow bark. Without him, that vial looks like poison.

scandal.text: Taylor rigged her own charity auction with a friendly bidder to make the total look bigger.

memories: You smuggled a bottle of your father's surgical spirit into the séance, because Griff's book said it would make the candles burn blue. You poured it into a saucer on the desk. When the candles went over, the spirit went up in a sheet of flame. You were nine years old, and you knew exactly what was in that bottle.

s1.truth: In my place on the south side, between Grant and Griff.
s1.lie: I went to the side table for my reticule.

s2.truth: Grant on one side, Griff on the other.
s2.lie: My husband was holding my hand.

s3.truth: At the inn last night he thanked me for the headache remedy. He said I had a kinder hand than I let people see.

s4.truth: Silas was unwell at the inn and asked me privately for a remedy. Feverfew and willow bark. I put a few drops in his glass.
s4.lie: I was at home pressing flowers.

s5.truth: I heard a little metallic scrape from the altar when the lights went out. I'm sure of it.

characters.blackout: In the dark you heard a thin metallic scrape from the direction of the altar, the sound of something lifted off a stand.
characters.last_word: Someone saw you put a vial in Silas's drink. Silas is the only person who could prove what was in it.

characters.intro: Baron Nanor Percival Ravenscroft. Financier. You may have heard of my investments; you certainly will before the night is out. I have money in railways, rubber, mines in places I can't pronounce, and a very promising scheme involving Peruvian guano. I am, as they say in the City, liquid. Extremely liquid. Practically a waterfall. Tonight I intend to make a modest fortune, a few friends, and a great deal of noise about both.

secret.title: The Clerk's Ledger
secret.text: When £8,000 went missing from your bank's accounts, you altered the ledger so the blame fell on your clerk, Edwin Marsh. He was dismissed and blacklisted across the City. The money was yours to explain, and you had spent it. Later you burned the one page that would have cleared him.
secret.excuse: Marsh was careless anyway. The bank would have collapsed and taken a hundred families with it. You protected far more people than you hurt.
secret.proof: A copy of the original ledger page, made by Marsh before it disappeared.

characters.need_alive: Silas knows of a dormant Ravenscroft claim on the estate trust that could rescue your finances. Only he can find the paperwork.

scandal.text: Griff published another scholar's history of the Hanseatic League as his own.

memories: You were the lookout at the far end of the passage. You saw the first flames, and you ran: not to the grown-ups, but to your own room, where you climbed into bed and pretended to be asleep. If you had shouted, the adults would have come five minutes sooner. You have done the arithmetic many times.

s1.truth: In my place on the north side, between Taylor and Danielle.
s1.lie: I went to the door to call for the footman.

s2.truth: Taylor and Danielle, either side of me.
s2.lie: My wife, who never lets go of my arm.

s3.truth: He told me the solicitor was right and I should stop shouting. I did not stop shouting.
s3.lie: He congratulated me on my investments.

s4.truth: I argued with the solicitor, Mr Thimble, about our family's claim to part of this estate. I said some things about obstacles disappearing. Legal obstacles.
s4.lie: I dined alone at my club.

s5.truth: I asked Silas what it was worth. He said, 'More than you can afford, my lord.' Cheek.

characters.blackout: A robe brushed hard across the back of your hand in the dark, someone moving fast. You smelled nothing, saw nothing, and grabbed at nothing.
characters.last_word: Silas knows what you did to Edwin Marsh. He also knows the one claim that could keep you solvent.

characters.intro: Lady Taylor Ravenscroft, philanthropist. I chair eleven committees, nine of which I founded, and two of which exist mainly to keep the other nine in order. I have raised money for orphans, widows, fallen women, distressed gentlefolk and, on one occasion, a donkey. I believe good manners are the foundation of civilisation, and I will be correcting yours all evening, purely out of love. Elbows off the table, Griffin.

secret.title: The Aunt's Last Will
secret.text: Sitting with your dying Aunt Hester, you found a new will in her writing box leaving her fortune to a children's hospital. You burned it in the grate. The older will, leaving everything to you, stood, and it has kept the Ravenscrofts afloat.
secret.excuse: Aunt Hester was confused at the end. The new will was a whim of her nurse's making. You only kept the family's money in the family.
secret.proof: The attendant's diary: 'Lady Taylor alone with the writing box. A smell of burning paper.'

characters.need_alive: Silas knows a witness who could show Aunt Hester was not of sound mind that week, which would mean you had done nothing so very wrong.

scandal.text: Danielle has been sending romantic poems, under a false name, to somebody else's husband.

memories: You were the keeper of the candles. You lit every one of them, more than a dozen, crowded together on the old desk among the papers, because it looked so beautiful in the dark. Nanny had told you a hundred times never to leave a flame beside paper. You have always told yourself that someone else knocked them over, so it couldn't have been your fault.

s1.truth: In my place at the west end of the north side, next to Nanor.
s1.lie: I went to the side table to find a candle.

s2.truth: Nanor. He was next to me.
s2.lie: Everyone could see me. I was standing up straight.

s3.truth: He returned the money my intermediary had offered him. He said, 'I'll be there tomorrow, Lady Taylor. I've waited twenty-five years.'
s3.lie: We talked about the seating plan.

s4.truth: I paid a man to persuade Silas to stay away from tonight. Silas always favoured Jonathan, and I didn't want him tipping the scales.
s4.lie: I was at a charity committee meeting.

s5.truth: I saw Silas straighten it on its stand three times. He was nervous. Silas is never nervous.

characters.blackout: Somewhere across the circle, a chair creaked as if someone had stood up or sat down. Then the thunder covered everything.
characters.last_word: You tried to keep Silas away from tonight. If anyone finds out, it will look like you knew what he was planning.

characters.intro: Professor Griffin Thaddeus Wraithmore, historian and explorer. I have crossed the Atlas Mountains, lectured to the Royal Geographical Society, and been bitten by a camel in front of the Khedive of Egypt. All true. Mostly true. True in spirit. I have known everyone in this room since we were children, and I have a story about each of you, which I shall tell at the worst possible moment. Do stop me if you've heard this one. You won't have.

secret.title: The Abandoned Companion
secret.text: On the 1886 Atlas expedition, your colleague Dr Samuel Okafor broke his leg in a snowbound pass. You left him behind to save yourself. Shepherds found him days later. He lived, but lost the leg and his career, while you published a heroic account claiming you had gone back for him.
secret.excuse: Two men would have died. Somebody had to get out and raise the alarm. You simply improved the story afterwards, as historians do.
secret.proof: Dr Okafor's own logbook from the pass, which contradicts every word of your book.

characters.need_alive: Silas can find the expedition's surviving guide before the Royal Geographical Society's inquiry next month. That guide could save you or ruin you.

scandal.text: Jonathan's 'ancient' family pedigree has a forged branch: the Norman knight never existed.

memories: The night of the fire was your idea. You had read about a séance in one of your father's forbidden books, and you dared the others to hold one in the locked records room of the east wing. When little Eleanor Vale said she was frightened, you called her a baby until she came along. You have spent twenty-five years telling yourself it was only a game.

s1.truth: In my place on the south side, between Caroline and Grace.
s1.lie: I went to the window to look at the storm.

s2.truth: Caroline and my wife, either side of me.
s2.lie: My wife was holding my hand.

s3.truth: He asked whether I still had my notebooks from the summer of '67. I said I might.
s3.lie: We discussed the Atlas Mountains. At length.

s4.truth: I paid two local toughs to recover my expedition instruments from the man who stole them. The target was the thief, not Silas.

s5.truth: I told Silas it was a reproduction. He agreed, cheerfully. Grace was furious with me for spoiling it.

characters.blackout: In the dark, close by the altar, you heard Silas whisper a single word: 'Eleanor.'
characters.last_word: Silas has Okafor's logbook. He also knows where the one witness who could save you is living.

characters.intro: Lady Grace Wraithmore. I collect antiquities: Roman bronzes, Egyptian scarabs, Etruscan mirrors, and grudges, which keep better than any of them. My husband discovers things; I acquire them, which is far more civilised. I can tell a forgery across a ballroom, and I can tell when someone is lying across a dinner table, so do sit somewhere else. I'm delighted to be here. I'm always delighted. You can tell by my face.

secret.title: The Child in the East Wing
secret.text: In the fire of 1867 you were the last one into the passage. Behind you, through the smoke, you heard Eleanor calling your name. You could have gone back for her. You ran. Afterwards you told everyone the room was already full of fire. It wasn't.
secret.excuse: You were a frightened child. Nobody blames a child. You tell yourself that nobody blames a child.
secret.proof: A statement you gave the parents' private inquiry in 1867, in your own childish hand, that contradicts what you told everyone else.

characters.need_alive: Silas alone can tell you whether a rescue would really have been possible. You have needed to know for twenty-five years.

scandal.text: Caroline has been sending herself anonymous love letters to make Grant jealous.

memories: You were the last one into the passage. Behind you, through the smoke, you heard Eleanor calling your name. You did not go back. Afterwards you told everyone the room was already full of fire. It wasn't.

s1.truth: In my place at the west end of the south side, next to Griff.
s1.lie: I went to the vestry door. It was banging.

s2.truth: Griff. My husband. Which I appreciate is not ideal.

s3.truth: He asked me, very gently, whether I still dream about the fire. I left the room.

s4.truth: I threw some old letters in the river. My parents' letters, about a private arrangement with another Order family. The red on the cloth was sealing-wax pigment, not blood.
s4.lie: I was at home with a headache.

s5.truth: I examined it before the ceremony. The blade is blunt. Ceremonial. You couldn't cut butter with it.

characters.blackout: You felt cold air on the back of your neck: the vestry door had blown open behind you, and then slammed shut in the wind.
characters.last_word: Silas knows you could have saved Eleanor. If anyone here had a reason to dread tonight, it was you.

witness_network.subject: grant
witness_network.saw: Last night you saw Grant in the manor basement with the cover off the new electrical panel, working at the fuses. When footsteps came down the stairs he ducked behind the coal bunker and hid until they had gone.
witness_network.truth: Last night you went down to the basement electrical panel. The exterior lamps were failing and you needed them on to survey the grounds after dark, so you fixed a loose fuse. You hid when someone came because it isn't your house and you didn't want to explain yourself to Jonathan.

witness_network.subject: grace
witness_network.saw: Last night at dusk you saw Grace on the river bridge, alone, throwing a bundle of papers and a cloth stained red into the water. She watched until it sank.
witness_network.truth: Last night you threw a bundle of old letters into the river. They documented your parents' private arrangement with another Order family, and you were not going to let anyone find them. The red on the wrapping cloth was old sealing-wax pigment, not blood.

witness_network.subject: jonathan
witness_network.saw: Last night, behind the Black Hound inn, you heard Jonathan say to Silas: 'If you tell them what you know, I'll make certain you never speak again.'
witness_network.truth: Last night you confronted Silas behind the Black Hound. You had hidden an old beneficiary schedule that suggests the Ravenscrofts have a claim to part of the estate, and Silas demanded you disclose it before the ceremony. You threatened him in anger, afraid of losing the manor. You had no idea what else he was planning.

witness_network.subject: nanor
witness_network.saw: Last night, through the inn parlour door, you heard Nanor arguing with the solicitor, Mr Thimble, about who owns this manor. Nanor said: 'Anything, or anyone, standing between me and my claim will have to disappear.'
witness_network.truth: Last night you argued with Mr Thimble the solicitor. You believe the Ravenscrofts have a genuine claim to part of the estate and you demanded he recognise it. The 'obstacles' you wanted gone were documents and lawyers.

witness_network.subject: griff
witness_network.saw: Last night in the inn yard you saw Griff hand money to two rough-looking men and tell them: 'Break a few bones if you have to.' You couldn't hear who they were meant to find.
witness_network.truth: Last night you paid two local toughs to recover your expedition instruments, worth a small fortune, from the man who stole them. The bones in question belonged to the thief, not to Silas.

witness_network.subject: caroline
witness_network.saw: Last night at the inn you saw Caroline tip a small vial into Silas's glass when she thought nobody was looking.
witness_network.truth: Last night Silas was unwell at the inn and asked you privately for something for his headache. You gave him a tincture of feverfew and willow bark, a few drops in his glass, at his request.

witness_network.subject: taylor
witness_network.saw: Last night in the churchyard you saw Taylor hand money to a stranger and say: 'Make sure Silas does not come tomorrow.'
witness_network.truth: Last night you paid an intermediary to persuade Silas to stay away from tonight. Silas favoured Jonathan when you were children and you didn't want him tipping the scales during the ceremony. Silas sent the money back.

witness_network.subject: danielle
witness_network.saw: Last night you saw Danielle come out of Silas's rooms above the post office carrying a small wooden box, looking over her shoulder.
witness_network.truth: Last night you collected a family heirloom from Silas's rooms: your grandmother's sapphire brooch, which you had quietly pawned and then redeemed through Silas. The box holds only the brooch and the pawn receipt. Jonathan doesn't know about the debt.

jonathan.weapon: the heavy iron key to the chapel, which you carry as master of the house

danielle.weapon: a jewelled stiletto hairpin from your collection, eight inches long

grant.weapon: your surveyor's steel plumb bob on its cord

griff.weapon: the bone-handled knife you carried across the Atlas

grace.weapon: a bronze Egyptian scarab paperweight from your collection

Who is most likely to wear their costume at home for fun?

What happened in your last conversation with Silas?

What did you see near the dagger?

summons.title: What Silas said when you arrived
summons.text: Silas Vale welcomed you home to Hollowmere. Your parents, the founders of the secret society known as the Hollow Order, entrusted him with one final duty: the reading of their true and final will. Before it can be read, the Order's tradition demands that all eight heirs take part in the Ceremony of the Covenant, in robes.

revelation.title: What Silas revealed when the lights went out
revelation.text: When the lights went out, Silas came back a different man. Eleanor, his little sister, died in the east-wing fire of 1867. Your parents called it an accident, and buried the truth: every one of you played a part in her death. Your parents left Silas the power to decide how their £12 million is shared, judged by your character, your loyalty and your actions. He knows your darkest secrets and means to bring them into the light. You will judge one another. Four families, but only three will inherit: one family will leave with nothing.

register.title: The Covenant register
register.text: The register each guest signed tonight on entering the chapel. It records the hand each member signed with, their chair in the ceremonial circle (north or south arc) and the sigil embroidered on their robe.

dagger_stand.title: The ceremonial dagger
dagger_stand.text: Photographed on its stand beside the altar at two minutes past nine. Fourteen inches, broad ceremonial blade.

scene.title: The scene
scene.text: When the lights returned, Silas Vale lay dead at the foot of the altar. The ceremonial dagger was gone from its stand. Everyone was where they had been standing before the lights went out. Or said they were.

instructions.title: Silas's sealed instructions
instructions.text: Found in Silas's desk, signed and witnessed before tonight's ceremony: 'Should I die before my judgment is made, the heirs shall decide it themselves. If they convict the one who killed me, that heir's family forfeits its inheritance entirely. If they fail, the family lowest in the Order's standings forfeits instead. The remaining three families shall divide the estate according to those standings.'

storm.title: The cause of the blackout
storm.text: The groundsman reports that lightning struck the generator house at nine minutes past nine. The fuses blew all at once. Nobody needed to touch the panel to cause it.

reunion.title: The Reunion
reunion.text: Welcome to Hollowmere. Each guest, in turn, introduce yourself to the room.
reunion.silas: Good evening, my lords, my ladies. Coats to me, quarrels to Sir Jonathan. Dinner is at nine, the sherry is now, and the east wing is still haunted, so I'd stay out of it.

polls.title: Who's Most Likely To…?
polls.text: Vote for the real person, not their character! Answer privately on your phone. The results go up on the screen.

covenant.title: The Ceremony of the Covenant
covenant.screen: THE CEREMONY OF THE COVENANT — ALL HEIRS MUST DON THEIR ROBES.
covenant.direction: Warm, affectionate, teasing: the beloved family servant.

sequence.say:
Ah, there you all are!

My goodness. Look at you.

It seems like only yesterday you were eight little troublemakers running through these halls.

And now look at you! Distinguished gentlemen, beautiful ladies... well, most of you anyway.

Now, I imagine you're all rather eager to learn why you've been summoned to Hollowmere Manor.

As you know, your parents were the founding members of a rather exclusive society known as The Hollow Order.

And before their passing, they entrusted me with one final responsibility.

The reading of their true and final will.

But, as I'm sure you remember, your parents were rather fond of their peculiar traditions.

And this occasion is no exception!

Before the will can be unveiled, the Hollow Order requires that all eight heirs participate in the traditional Ceremony of the Covenant.

Yes, I'm afraid that means the robes.

Do put them on, won't you?

I promise, you'll all look absolutely ridiculous.

Once everyone is properly dressed, we shall begin the reading of the will.

And perhaps, at long last, discover what your dear parents have left you.
Come along, then. Let's not keep the dead waiting.

sequence.text: THE CEREMONY OF THE COVENANT — ALL HEIRS MUST DON THEIR ROBES.

covenant2.title: The True Covenant Has Begun
covenant2.direction: Controlled, wounded, occasionally wickedly funny. He blames all eight for Eleanor's accidental death. He is still alive.

sequence.say:
Ahhh.

There we are.

Eight heirs of the Hollow Order.

Standing proudly in the very robes your parents once wore.

How splendid.

How utterly revolting.

Twenty-five years.

Twenty-five long years I've waited to see you all standing here together again.

Do any of you remember Eleanor?

My little sister.

She loved this manor. She loved your families.

And she adored every single one of you.

Until that dreadful night in 1867.

The fire.

The screaming.

The east wing engulfed in flames.

And my dear Eleanor... trapped inside.

Your parents called it a tragic accident.

An unfortunate twist of fate.

And for years, I believed them.
But I know the truth now.

sequence.text: Every single one of you played a part in my sister's death.

sequence.say: Every single one of you played a part in my sister's death.

Perhaps none of you intended for her to die.

Perhaps you were simply foolish children.

But your parents knew what happened.

And rather than admit the truth, they buried it.

They protected their precious family names.

And left me to bury my sister.

For twenty-five years, I've served your families.

Poured your wine.

Polished your silver.

Smiled politely while you grew into the very people your parents raised you to be.

And all the while...

I remembered.

But enough about the past.

Let's discuss your future.

Or rather...
Your inheritance.

Twelve million pounds.

A magnificent fortune left behind by the founding members of the Hollow Order.

And do you know the most delightful part?

Your parents entrusted me with deciding how it should be distributed.

Not equally. Oh, heavens no.

They instructed me to judge their children by their values, their character, their loyalty...

And their actions.

Imagine that.

After a lifetime of taking orders from your families...

I finally get to decide what you're worth.

And I've devised a rather special evening to help me reach my decision.

You see, I know things about each of you.

Terrible things.

Secrets you've hidden from your friends.

From your spouses.

Perhaps even from yourselves.

And tonight, I intend to bring those secrets into the light.

You will judge one another.

You will decide who is trustworthy, who is loyal, and who deserves a share of your parents' fortune.

And I shall be watching.

Every accusation.

Every betrayal.

Every desperate attempt to protect your precious reputations.

Four families.

Twelve million pounds.

But only three families shall inherit.
One family will leave this manor with absolutely nothing.

Your parents took something from me that no amount of money could ever replace.

Tonight, I intend to return the favor.

Oh, don't look so frightened.

I'm not a monster.

I'm merely the man who's been serving your dinner for twenty-five years.

And tonight...

I'm serving something rather different.

ballot1.title: The First Inheritance Ballot
ballot1.screen: Rank three fellow guests on your phone. Not yourself. Not your spouse. Last place inherits nothing.
ballot1.silas:
Now then, my dear friends.

Let us discuss something far more pleasant.

Twelve million pounds.

Four families. One extraordinary fortune.

But which family deserves the lion's share?

That, my dear heirs, is entirely up to you.

Throughout tonight's proceedings, you will be asked to judge one another.

Not by your titles, your fortunes, or the reputations of your parents...

But by your character.

Who among you is most trustworthy?

Who has shown the greatest loyalty?

And who, quite frankly, deserves to walk away with the most money?

Each of you must rank three fellow guests in order of who you believe is most deserving.

Your first choice receives the greatest favor, followed by your second and third.

You may not vote for yourself.

And you may not vote for your spouse.

After all, even the Hollow Order has standards when it comes to favoritism.

Your votes will determine each family's standing and how much of the fortune they stand to inherit.

But there is one rather unfortunate detail I neglected to mention...

The family that finishes in last place shall inherit absolutely nothing.

Not a penny.

The remaining three families will divide the entire twelve million pounds.

So choose your loyalties wisely.

A vote for a friend may cost your family a fortune.

And a misplaced act of kindness could leave you walking out of Hollowmere Manor...

Completely penniless.

Your loyalties may change as the evening unfolds.

I suspect they will.

So look around this room.

Consider the people you've known since childhood.

Who would you trust with your life?

And more importantly...

Who would you trust with twelve million pounds?

Let the voting begin.

murder.title: THE HOLLOW ORDER SEES ALL
murder.text: Last night, every person in this room was involved in something suspicious. Every secret has a witness. And now, one of you is a murderer. What you choose to reveal, and what you choose to conceal, is entirely up to you. Let the accusations begin.

ghost.title: Death does not release you from the Covenant
ghost.silas: Did you think a blade would end it? I am still here. I am in the walls and the wires and the glass. The Covenant stands. Find the one who killed my sister, and me. I will be watching.

ballots2.title: Inheritance and Suspicion
ballots2.text: Rank three guests for the inheritance, then rank your three prime suspects. Every point of suspicion costs the accused influence.

deals.title: The Dinner of Deception
deals.text: The first deals may now be struck. Pay for protection, or pay to force a question. Every promise can be broken.

interrogations.title: The Order's Inquisition
interrogations.text: One interrogation each, in order of influence.

investigations.title: Private Investigations
investigations.text: Each couple may investigate one guest in secret. The guest will be told only what is being looked into.

bribes4.title: A Word in Your Ear
bribes4.text: Offers may now be made for inheritance votes. Only inheritance votes.

ballots3.title: Inheritance and Suspicion
ballots3.text: The third inheritance ballot, and the second suspicion ballot.

revelations.title: Silas's Revenge
revelations.silas: You lied to me. Some of you, a great deal. You also paid each other. Let us see who.

temptation.title: The Last Temptation
temptation.text: The final chance to buy an inheritance vote.

ballot4.title: The Final Inheritance Ballot
ballot4.text: Your last inheritance vote. Suspicion will still cost influence.

hotseat.title: The Devil's Defense
hotseat.text: The two prime suspects take the hot seat. Each may defend themselves, or accuse another.

suspicion3.title: The Final Suspicion Ballot
suspicion3.text: Rank your three suspects for the last time.

bridge.title: The Ghost Remembers
bridge.silas: I cannot tell you who. The dead are not permitted. But I can show you what my sister saw, and what my hand closed on as I fell.

wagers.title: The Devil's Wager
wagers.text: Wager on the accused: guilty, or not guilty. Up to a quarter of your family's share.

verdict.title: The Final Tribunal
verdict.text: Four votes of eight convict. Vote YES or NO.
